choices: Checking her airway, breathing, and circulation
Making sure the scene is safe for you and your crew
Getting a full set of vital signs
questions.explanation: Scene safety is the first concern on any call, before assessment or vitals. You cannot help the patient if you or your crew get hurt walking in.
questions.question: You push open the door of a small motel room where a sick woman is lying in bed and a man is standing nearby. Before you walk in and start care, what has to come first?

choices: Keep working around it so the patient is not delayed
Ask the patient to move the hazard out of the way
Back out to a safe area and call for the appropriate resources to handle the hazard
Ignore it as long as the patient looks stable
questions.explanation: If a hazard can be made safe without endangering anyone, make it safe. If it cannot, retreat to a safe area and call for the right resources to deal with it.
questions.question: Partway through a call you spot a hazard in the room that you cannot make safe without putting yourself or someone else at risk. What should you do?

choices: The shopping cart nearby proves he is homeless and nothing else is going on
His disheveled look tells you alcohol is the only possible cause
A patient found beside a road is always a trauma patient
His spot beside the road raises the possibility of trauma, and traffic is a hazard you will have to guard against
questions.explanation: Position beside the road suggests possible trauma, and the roadside itself is a traffic hazard for patient and providers. The cart and his appearance hint at homelessness, but you must not settle on those as the only possibilities.
questions.question: You are dispatched to a viaduct for an unresponsive man, and a homeless camp with a recent tuberculosis outbreak is not far away. Before you ever greet the patient, what can a quick survey of the scene already tell you?

questions.explanation: Situational awareness is knowledge of your surroundings and the ability to recognize potential risks to the patient or the EMS team.
questions.question: Good crews keep track of what is going on around them for the whole call — the crowd, the traffic, the exits — so a risk does not sneak up on them. That habit of knowing your surroundings and spotting risks early is called:

questions.explanation: Personal protective equipment is the protective gear that blocks exposure to a pathogen or hazardous material. Standard precautions are the routine measures behind using it on every call.
questions.question: Because the camp near the viaduct has had a tuberculosis outbreak, you put on gloves and a HEPA mask before you touch the patient. Gloves, masks, and other gear designed to block your exposure to a pathogen or hazardous material are collectively called:

questions.explanation: The primary assessment is the step that identifies and initiates treatment of immediate and potential life threats. The detailed exam and repeat checks come later.
questions.question: In the first minute with a new patient, your main job is the step whose whole purpose is to find and start treating immediate life threats. That step is the:

questions.explanation: She opens her eyes when you speak to her, so she is responding to verbal stimuli — your voice — not to pain.
questions.question: The woman in the motel room opens her eyes when you speak to her. Based on that response, she is responsive to:

choices: It gives you clues about what is causing the problem and how stable he is, and it guides your treatment and the hospital's decisions
It replaces the need to take a history
It lets you name the exact disease before transport
It only matters when the patient can talk to you
questions.explanation: Assessment provides clues to the cause of the patient's problem and how serious or stable he is. It guides prehospital treatment and helps hospital staff make decisions if he is transported.
questions.question: On the viaduct call you know almost nothing about the unresponsive man at first. Why is a careful, skilled assessment so important on a call like this?

choices: Patients always lie about what happened
Even a patient who can talk may not know about problems like hypoxia, low blood sugar, internal bleeding, or a brain injury — and this man cannot answer at all
Talking to the patient delays the primary assessment, which is the only step that matters
Life threats can only be found once he reaches the hospital
questions.explanation: A patient may be unaware of hypoxia, hypoglycemia, cardiac dysrhythmias, internal bleeding, shock, or brain injury, and a nonverbal patient cannot answer at all. Further assessment is essential to find life threats.
questions.question: Your partner says, "Let's just ask him what happened and we'll know if anything life-threatening is going on." Why is that not enough with this patient?

questions.explanation: The general impression is the overall initial impression that determines the priority for patient care, based on surroundings, mechanism of injury, signs and symptoms, and chief complaint.
questions.question: As you walk up to a patient, you take in his surroundings, how he looks, and what seems to be wrong, and you form a quick overall picture that sets the priority for his care. That first overall picture is your:

questions.explanation: AVPU grades consciousness as alert, responds to verbal stimuli, responds to pain, or unresponsive. Reacting only when you apply a painful stimulus puts him at P.
questions.question: Near the end of the transport, the unresponsive man does not react to your voice anymore, but he pulls back when you press hard on his nail bed with your pen. On the AVPU scale, he is at:

choices: Tenderness in the right lower abdomen that you found on exam
questions.explanation: The chief complaint is the reason the patient called for help, in the patient's own terms. She reports fever and chills; the tenderness and vital signs are findings you discovered, not her stated reason for calling.
questions.question: You ask the motel patient what brought on the call for help, and she describes how she has been feeling for several days. Which of these is her chief complaint — the reason she called, in her own terms?
questions.topic: History taking and the chief complaint

questions.explanation: Pertinent negatives are negative findings that warrant no care or intervention. Documenting what the patient does not have still helps narrow the picture.
questions.question: As you take the motel patient's history, she tells you she has no chest pain and no trouble breathing, and neither answer changes what you will do for her. Negative findings like that — things she does not have, which need no care or intervention — are called:
questions.topic: History taking and the chief complaint

questions.explanation: SAMPLE walks you through signs and symptoms, allergies, medications, pertinent past history, last oral intake, and events leading up to the call, so you can resume the history even after an interruption.
questions.question: You are partway through asking the motel patient about her allergies and medications when you have to stop and treat her. Later, a simple memory aid helps you pick the history questions back up without missing any. That aid is:
questions.topic: History taking and the chief complaint

choices: His chief complaint is alcohol use, so he is a medical patient
Without a stated complaint there is no chief complaint, so he defaults to a trauma patient
The rifampin prescription makes tuberculosis his chief complaint
His chief complaint is his unresponsiveness itself, and at this point you cannot conclude whether he is a medical or a trauma patient
questions.explanation: Unconsciousness itself can be a chief complaint. His decreased mental status could come from alcohol, hypoxia, or a seizure (medical), or from a brain injury after a fall or being struck by a car (trauma), so the category is not yet conclusive.
questions.question: The unresponsive man never states a complaint of his own. What is his chief complaint, and what does it mean for sorting him as a medical or trauma patient?
questions.topic: History taking and the chief complaint

questions.explanation: OPQRST stands for onset, provocation/palliation, quality, region/radiation, severity, and timing — the standard framework for evaluating a patient's pain.
questions.question: A patient with chest pain is describing it to you, and you work through when it started, what brings it on or eases it, what it feels like, where it is and whether it spreads, how bad it is, and how long it has been going on. That set of pain questions is organized by:
questions.topic: History taking and the chief complaint

questions.explanation: History taking is the step that provides details about the patient's chief complaint and further insight into the nature of the illness, after immediate life threats have been addressed.
questions.question: After the primary assessment on a responsive patient, you settle in to get the details behind her chief complaint — the step that fills in her story and gives you further insight into the nature of her illness. That step is:
questions.topic: History taking and the chief complaint

questions.explanation: Orientation is mental status measured by memory of person, place, time, and event — exactly the four things those questions test.
questions.question: You ask a patient his name, where he is right now, roughly what day and time it is, and what happened to him. You are checking his:
questions.topic: History taking and the chief complaint

questions.explanation: The field impression is your conclusion about the cause of the patient's condition after considering the situation, history, and scene. The general impression comes earlier, at first contact.
questions.question: You have looked at the scene, heard the history, and weighed all the findings, and now you settle on what you believe is causing the patient's condition. That conclusion is your:
questions.topic: History taking and the chief complaint

choices: The scene survey, the physical exam, and his vital signs
SAMPLE answers supplied by the police officer
The dispatch information from the caller
questions.explanation: When the patient cannot give a history, the only information available is the scene survey, the physical exam, and vital signs. Those clues drive your judgment of his stability and possible causes.
questions.question: With no history available from the unresponsive man — he cannot answer SAMPLE or OPQRST questions — where do your working clues have to come from?

choices: Crackles always mean tuberculosis, so he is a medical patient
They will not sort themselves out — the same findings could come from medical causes like pneumonia or tuberculosis, or from trauma like a lung injury or internal bleeding
A swollen abdomen always means internal bleeding from trauma
Bloody sputum rules out a medical cause
questions.explanation: Problems are not always clear, especially with no history. The lung sounds could be tuberculosis, pneumonia, or pneumothorax; the distention could be trauma, internal bleeding, or an enlarged liver from alcoholism.
questions.question: En route with the unresponsive man, you find decreased breath sounds low on the right, crackles low on the left, what looks like bloody sputum on his shirt, and a mildly swollen abdomen. What do these findings tell you about sorting out his problem?

choices: Sit him up so he can cough more easily and remove the nasal airway
Skip the mask, since tuberculosis has not been confirmed
Keep a mask on because untreated tuberculosis is possible, continue oxygen and airway care, consider a cervical collar for possible head and spine injury, and keep him warm and supine
Delay transport until the cause is pinned down
questions.explanation: With an unclear cause you treat the possibilities: mask up for possible untreated tuberculosis, keep managing airway and oxygen in case hypoxia is involved, consider a collar for possible head and spinal trauma, and keep him warm and supine against possible internal injury or shock.
questions.question: The cause of the man's unconsciousness is still unclear. Which set of actions fits what you should be doing for him?

choices: Write "no change" and leave the numbers out
Record the vital signs you expect him to have on arrival
Note only the nail bed response, since unchanged vitals do not need documenting
Write the vital signs exactly as you measured them, and note that he now responds to pain and still tolerates the nasal airway and oxygen mask
questions.explanation: Document the vital signs directly as obtained, along with the observations that he has become responsive to pain and continues to tolerate the nasal airway and oxygen mask. "No change" without numbers is not a record.
questions.question: His repeat vital signs look about the same as your baseline set, though he now responds when you press on a nail bed. How should that go in your report?

choices: At least every 15 minutes, and every 5 minutes if they start to destabilize
Once more before arrival is enough
Every 30 minutes, since he looks stable
Only when his mental status changes
questions.explanation: Vital signs should be repeated at least every 15 minutes. If they start to destabilize, increase the frequency to every 5 minutes or as often as the situation allows.
questions.question: How often should you repeat the unresponsive man's vital signs during this transport?

choices: Rechecking his pupils and nothing else
A repeat Glasgow Coma Scale score and a blood glucose reading
A second SAMPLE history taken from the police officer
Listening to the same breath sounds again and nothing else
questions.explanation: A repeated GCS score tracks his mental status over time, and a blood glucose reading can reveal hypoglycemia or hyperglycemia as a cause of unresponsiveness. Pulse oximetry and, with ALS, capnography add further information.
questions.question: Over the next few minutes before arrival, which added checks would give you the most useful new information about this unresponsive man?

questions.explanation: A focused assessment is performed on patients with nonsignificant mechanisms of injury or on responsive medical patients, and it concentrates on the area of the patient's complaint.
questions.question: A responsive medical patient twisted her ankle in a minor fall and complains only of ankle pain. Instead of a head-to-toe workup, you examine the area she is complaining about, guided by her signs and symptoms. That kind of exam is a:

questions.explanation: DCAP-BTLS stands for deformities, contusions, abrasions, punctures/penetrations, burns, tenderness, lacerations, and swelling — the findings you check for in each body area.
questions.question: During a trauma exam you check each area of the body for deformities, contusions, abrasions, punctures or penetrations, burns, tenderness, lacerations, and swelling. That checklist of what to look for is remembered as:

questions.explanation: A rapid heart rate over 100 beats/min is tachycardia. Bradycardia is a slow rate, and tachypnea and dyspnea describe breathing, not pulse.
questions.question: The motel patient's pulse comes back at 140 beats/min. A heart rate that fast is best described as:

questions.explanation: Systolic pressure is the increased pressure in an artery with each contraction of the ventricles (systole), and it is the top number of a blood pressure reading. The bottom number is the diastolic pressure.
questions.question: You take a blood pressure of 142/96 on the unresponsive man. The top number, 142, is the increased pressure in the artery that comes with each contraction of the ventricles. That top number is the:

questions.explanation: The mean arterial pressure is the average pressure in the circulatory system during one cardiac cycle, blending the systolic peak and the diastolic resting pressure.
questions.question: One calculated value gives you the average pressure in the whole circulatory system across one full cardiac cycle. That value is the:

choices: Blood draining back toward the heart through the veins
Air moving through the artery with each breath
The wave of pressure created as the heart contracts and forces blood out of the left ventricle into the major arteries
questions.explanation: A pulse is the wave of pressure created as the heart contracts and forces blood out of the left ventricle and into the major arteries. That wave is what your fingers detect at the wrist.
questions.question: At the unresponsive man's wrist you feel a strong, rhythmic throb each time his heart beats. What you are feeling is:

questions.explanation: Perfusion is the flow of blood through body tissues and vessels. Without it, tissues do not receive the oxygen the blood is carrying.
questions.question: However strong a patient's heart beats, what the tissues actually depend on is blood moving through them. The flow of blood through the body's tissues and vessels is called:

choices: Distal circulatory function — how well blood returns to the tissues after being squeezed out
questions.explanation: Capillary refill evaluates distal circulatory function by blanching blood from an area such as a nail bed and watching the speed of its return after you release the pressure.
questions.question: You squeeze a patient's fingertip until it blanches white, let go, and time how quickly the color returns. That test gives you a quick read on:

questions.explanation: Vasoconstriction is the narrowing of a blood vessel. It is one way the body redirects and conserves blood flow under stress.
questions.question: A cold, stressed patient's body narrows some of its blood vessels to keep more blood near the core. The narrowing of a blood vessel is called:

choices: Low pressure is hypertension; high pressure is hypotension
Both readings are just called blood pressure
Low pressure is bradycardia; high pressure is tachycardia
Low pressure is hypotension; high pressure is hypertension
questions.explanation: Blood pressure lower than the normal range is hypotension, and blood pressure higher than the normal range is hypertension. Bradycardia and tachycardia describe heart rate, not pressure.
questions.question: Two patients have their pressures taken at the same clinic. One reads well below the normal range and the other reads well above it. Which pairing names those two findings correctly?

questions.explanation: Bradycardia is a slow heart rate of less than 60 beats/min. Tachycardia is the opposite, a rate over 100 beats/min.
questions.question: A resting athlete on the bench has a pulse of 48 beats/min. A heart rate that slow — under 60 beats/min — is called:

questions.explanation: Vital signs are the key signs used to evaluate the patient's overall condition: respirations, pulse, blood pressure, level of consciousness, and skin characteristics.
questions.question: Before you leave the scene, you record a patient's respirations, pulse, blood pressure, level of consciousness, and skin color, temperature, and condition. Together, those key measurements used to evaluate the patient's overall condition are his:

questions.explanation: Pulse oximetry measures the oxygen saturation of hemoglobin in the capillary beds. In this case it helps show whether hypoxia is present and how saturation changes with oxygen.
questions.question: You clip a small probe onto the unresponsive man's finger and get a percentage for how saturated his hemoglobin is with oxygen. That assessment tool is:

questions.explanation: Capnography is a noninvasive method that quickly provides information on ventilatory status, arterial circulation, and tissue perfusion. ALS can use it to judge whether the patient is ventilating adequately.
questions.question: An ALS crew adds a sensor that gives a noninvasive, ongoing read on how well the patient is ventilating, how his arterial circulation is doing, and how well his tissues are perfused. That method is:

questions.explanation: Wheezing is a high-pitched, whistling breath sound, most prominent on expiration, that suggests obstruction or narrowing of the lower airways, as in asthma and bronchiolitis.
questions.question: Listening to a teenager with asthma, you hear a high-pitched, whistling sound, loudest as she breathes out, coming from narrowed lower airways. That sound is:

questions.explanation: Stridor is a harsh, high-pitched respiratory sound, generally heard during inspiration, caused by partial blockage or narrowing of the upper airway. It may be audible without a stethoscope.
questions.question: A toddler's breathing makes a harsh, high-pitched sound on the way in that you can hear without a stethoscope, pointing to a partial blockage up high in the airway. That sound is:

questions.explanation: Crackles are crackling, rattling breath sounds that signal fluid in the air spaces of the lungs. The unresponsive man in the case study had them in his left lower chest.
questions.question: Through your stethoscope you hear crackling, rattling sounds in a patient's lungs — the kind produced by fluid sitting in the air spaces of the lungs. Those sounds are:

questions.explanation: Rhonchi are coarse, low-pitched breath sounds heard in patients with chronic mucus in the upper airways. Crackles are finer and come from fluid down in the air spaces.
questions.question: An older man with a chronic cough has coarse, low-pitched breath sounds from mucus sitting in his upper airways. Those sounds are:

questions.explanation: Retractions are movements in which the skin pulls in around the ribs during inspiration — a sign the child is working hard to move air.
questions.question: A small child working hard to breathe has skin that pulls in around her ribs every time she breathes in. Those inward pulls are called:

questions.explanation: Nasal flaring is the widening of the nostrils, and it indicates that there is an airway obstruction. It is one of the visible signs of increased breathing effort.
questions.question: You notice a struggling infant's nostrils widening with each breath, a sign that air is not moving freely through the airway. That widening of the nostrils is called:

questions.explanation: Labored breathing is the use of the muscles of the chest, back, and abdomen — the accessory muscles, including the sternocleidomastoids and pectoralis major — to assist in expanding the chest when air movement is impaired.
questions.question: A man in respiratory distress is using his neck muscles, his chest muscles, and his abdominal muscles just to pull air in and push it out. Breathing that takes that kind of extra muscle work is described as:

questions.explanation: Shallow respirations are characterized by little movement of the chest wall (reduced tidal volume) or poor chest excursion, and they may come with other signs of inadequate breathing.
questions.question: The motel patient's respirations are 24 breaths/min, and her chest barely rises with each breath — the excursion looks poor and each breath moves very little air. Breathing like that is described as:

questions.explanation: Tidal volume is the amount of air, in milliliters, moved into or out of the lungs during one breath. Shallow breathing means that volume has dropped.
questions.question: Each breath a patient takes moves a certain amount of air into or out of the lungs, measured in milliliters. That amount of air per breath is the:

questions.explanation: Spontaneous respirations are breathing that occurs without assistance. Confirming he is breathing on his own tells you ventilation support can focus on oxygen and monitoring.
questions.question: After you open the unresponsive man's airway and place a nasopharyngeal airway, he is breathing on his own with no help from you or a bag-mask device. Breathing that occurs without assistance is called:

questions.explanation: The tripod position is an upright position in which the patient leans forward onto two arms stretched forward and thrusts the head and chin forward — a posture patients adopt when breathing is hard work.
questions.question: You find a breathless patient sitting upright, leaning forward onto both arms stretched out in front of him, with his head and chin thrust forward as he braces himself to breathe. That posture is the:

questions.explanation: Two- to three-word dyspnea is a severe breathing problem in which the patient can speak only two to three words at a time without pausing to take a breath. It is a quick, visible gauge of how bad the breathing problem is.
questions.question: A patient with a severe breathing problem can only get out two or three words at a time before he has to stop and take another breath. That finding is known as:

questions.explanation: The sniffing position is an upright position in which the patient's head and chin are thrust slightly forward to keep the airway open.
questions.question: To help keep a patient's airway open, you sit him upright and position his head with the chin thrust slightly forward. That head position is the:

choices: She says she has been vomiting
The man in the room says she has not eaten in two days
questions.explanation: A blood pressure of 100/60 mm Hg is a sign — an objective finding that can be measured. Her fever, chills, vomiting, and diarrhea are symptoms she reports, which makes them subjective.
questions.question: Which of these findings from the motel call is an objective finding — something you can see, hear, feel, or measure yourself?

choices: Skin that is hot to the touch and flushed
Chills she has been having for several days
questions.explanation: A symptom is a subjective finding the patient feels and only the patient can identify — her chills qualify. Hot skin, pulse, and respirations are things you can measure or feel yourself.
questions.question: Which of these from the motel call is a subjective finding — something the patient feels that only the patient can identify?

questions.explanation: The conjunctiva is the delicate membrane that lines the eyelids and covers the exposed surface of the eye — the same tissue that looked red in this patient. The sclera is the tough white portion beneath it.
questions.question: Examining the unresponsive man's eyes, you note redness in the delicate membrane that lines the eyelids and covers the exposed surface of the eye. That membrane is the:

questions.explanation: Jaundice is yellow skin or sclera caused by liver disease or dysfunction. The sclera is the white portion of the eye where the yellowing shows.
questions.question: A patient with liver disease has a yellow tint to his skin and to the whites of his eyes. That yellowing is called:

questions.explanation: Crepitus is a grating or grinding sensation or sound caused by fractured bone ends or joints rubbing together, felt or heard on examination.
questions.question: Running your hands over a patient's fractured leg, you feel a grating, grinding sensation as the broken bone ends rub together. That finding is:

questions.explanation: Subcutaneous emphysema is a characteristic crackling sensation felt on palpation of the skin, caused by air present in the soft tissues. It feels similar to crepitus, but the cause is trapped air, not bone ends.
questions.question: After a chest injury, palpating a patient's neck and upper chest gives you a crackling sensation under the skin, as if air were trapped in the soft tissues. That sensation is:

questions.explanation: Paradoxical motion is the motion of the detached portion of chest wall in a flail chest — in during inhalation and out during exhalation, opposite to the normal motion of the intact chest wall.
questions.question: In a patient with a flail chest, the detached section of the chest wall sinks in when he breathes in and pushes out when he breathes out — exactly opposite to the motion of the rest of the chest. That backwards movement is:

questions.explanation: Guarding is involuntary muscle contraction (spasm) of the abdominal wall to minimize the pain of abdominal movement, and it is a sign of peritonitis.
questions.question: A patient with a severe abdominal infection involuntarily tenses his abdominal wall into a spasm whenever you try to examine him, as if to keep the sore area from moving. That involuntary tensing is:

questions.explanation: Diaphoretic means characterized by light or profuse sweating. It is a skin finding you can observe during the primary assessment and vital signs.
questions.question: Your patient is pale and sweating profusely even though the room is cool. A patient who is sweating like that is described as:

questions.explanation: Cyanosis is a blue skin discoloration caused by a reduced level of oxygen in the blood. Like paleness, it signals a significant disruption of normal physiology.
questions.question: A patient's lips and nail beds have taken on a blue tint because the level of oxygen in her blood has dropped. That blue discoloration is:

questions.explanation: Altered mental status is a change in the way a person thinks and behaves that may signal disease in the central nervous system or elsewhere in the body. It is a finding, not a diagnosis.
questions.question: A normally sharp man is confused, slow to answer, and not thinking or behaving like himself — a change that can point to disease in the central nervous system or elsewhere in the body. That change is called:

questions.explanation: A distracting injury is any injury that prevents the patient from noticing other injuries he may have, such as a painful femur fracture masking back pain from a spinal injury. It is why you examine thoroughly instead of relying only on complaints.
questions.question: A man with a badly broken femur never mentions any back pain, even though he also has a spinal injury — the leg simply hurts so much more. An injury that keeps a patient from noticing other injuries, even severe ones, is a:

questions.explanation: The mechanism of injury is the forces, or energy transmission, applied to the body that cause injury. For a medical patient you would instead consider the nature of illness — the general type of illness he is experiencing.
questions.question: For the man found beside the road, you think about the forces that may have been applied to his body — a fall, or being struck by a car. The forces, or energy transmission, applied to the body that cause injury are the:

questions.explanation: Triage is the process of establishing treatment and transportation priorities according to severity of injury and medical condition, so limited resources go where they do the most good.
questions.question: At a bus crash with more patients than crews, you sort the patients and set treatment and transportation priorities according to how severe each person's injury or condition is. That sorting process is:

questions.explanation: The incident command system manages disasters and mass-casualty incidents, with section chiefs — finance, logistics, operations, and planning — reporting to the incident commander.
questions.question: At a large disaster, section chiefs for finance, logistics, operations, and planning all report to a single incident commander. That management system is the:

questions.explanation: The Golden Hour is the time from injury to definitive care, during which treatment of shock and traumatic injuries should begin as soon as possible; on-scene time for critical trauma patients should stay to 10 minutes or less.
questions.question: A trauma patient with life-threatening injuries needs definitive care fast. The concept that treatment of shock and traumatic injuries should begin as soon as possible, with 10 minutes or less spent on scene for patients with life- or limb-threatening injuries, is summed up as the:

questions.explanation: To auscultate is to listen to sounds within an organ with a stethoscope. Its hands-on counterpart, to palpate, means to examine by touch.
questions.question: You place your stethoscope on the unresponsive man's chest to listen to the sounds inside his lungs. Examining a patient by listening to sounds within an organ with a stethoscope is called:

questions.explanation: Metabolism is the biochemical process that results in production of energy from nutrients within the cells, also called cellular respiration. Perfusion delivers the blood; metabolism is what the cells do with what arrives.
questions.question: Inside a patient's cells, biochemical processes are turning nutrients into energy — the process also called cellular respiration. That production of energy is:

questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide typically makes up 0.03% of air at sea level and is the waste product exhaled during expiration by the respiratory system.
questions.question: The gas you exhale as a waste product of respiration — the same gas that normally makes up only about 0.03% of the air at sea level — is:

questions.explanation: Frostbite is damage to tissues as the result of exposure to cold; frozen or partially frozen body parts are frostbitten. It is a local injury, unlike a whole-body temperature drop.
questions.question: A man found outside in deep cold has fingers that are frozen and stiff from exposure — tissue damage caused by the cold itself. That injury is:

questions.explanation: Hypothermia is a condition in which the internal body temperature falls below 95°F (35°C). Frostbite, by contrast, is cold damage to a specific body part.
questions.question: Another patient pulled in from the cold has an internal body temperature of 94°F, below the 95°F (35°C) line. That whole-body condition is:
